We appreciate the reviewer iBiG for providing important follow up questions. We have several misunderstanding regarding the reviewer’s previous comments, and we sincerely apologize for this. We would like to provide additional responses to address the concerns.

**On the claim that introducing gaze “unavoidably impacts” fundamental capabilities**  

We initially thought the Limitation2 was more about adding gaze-independent questions to our benchmark. We want to make two clarifications:  
- **Gaze-Guided Prompting approach (main results)**: Our main method is the intent-guided prompting, where the model weights are *frozen* and gaze is incorporated purely via prompting. In this training-free setting, the original model’s general capabilities remain *unchanged*, while it gains the ability to answer gaze-related queries.  

- **Lora Fine-tuning experiments (analytic purpose)**: The LoRA fine-tuning is intended as an **analytic experiment** — to study potential overfitting and to encourage researchers to explore more effective training methods for addressing EgoGazeVQA without overfitting — rather than as the optimal solution to our task. In fact, how to design a training pipeline that boosts performance on EgoGazeVQA without losing generalization ability on other tasks is an important open challenge we aim to introduce to the community for future exploration. We will clarify this in the revision.  

- **Additonal Generalization experiments**: Though solving the generalization problem is beyond the scope of this benchmark paper, we provide an initial attempt to optimize the LoRA SFT training data to better balance performance on EgoGazeVQA and EgoSchema. Instead of training solely on video–question–answer pairs, which risks overfitting, we concatenated the text-based gaze-guided prompt (GazeT) with each question, enabling the model to learn meaningful knowledge for gaze-specific associations while reducing overfitting on general questions.

We applied this to Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and tested the model on EgoSchema for OOD generalization. Note that all LoRA SFT models are trained on EGTEA tested on Ego4D and EgoExo. The results are shown below:

| Methods       |SFT Data Question Format|  EgoSchema Avg(\%)  | EgoGazeVQA Avg(\%) |
| ------------- |---------------|-------------| ------------|
| Zero-shot 7B     |N/A            |  60.72 | 50.26|
| LoRA SFT  7B     |Question only  |  48.30 (-12.42) |68.85 (+18.59) |
| LoRA SFT  7B     |Textual Gaze Prompt + Question|  58.32 (-2.40)|67.00 (+16.74) |


For fair comparison, all above experiments from the above table are using textual gaze prompt (GazeV) for EgoGazeVQA. From the 7B model results, SFT using gaze-guided prompts together with questions helps mitigate overfitting compared with question-only training, achieving performance close to the original model on EgoSchema while also delivering notable improvements on EgoGazeVQA. Here, we focus on examining this data optimization strategy with textual gaze prompts (GazeT), and we will explore applying similar strategies to visual gaze prompt (GazeV) and sailency gaze prompt (GazeS) in future work.


**On models without gaze input being pointless for this benchmark**  

We initially thought the comment from Limitation 3 referred to the concern that performance trends in Tables 4 and 5 might mainly reflect the number of possible targets rather than true task complexity. We apologize for this misunderstanding. Our benchmark is intentionally designed to evaluate a specific capability: using gaze information to answer egocentric intent-related questions. Including results for models without gaze serves a **baseline function** — it quantifies the performance gap between models that can exploit gaze and those that cannot. These baselines help calibrate expectations and guide future development, similar to the reviewer’s helpful suggestion on Table 7 to add baseline results without gaze estimation to calibrate performance changes. We will make the design intent of this experiment clearer in the paper to avoid misinterpretation.  

**Summary:**  
1. Gaze-guided intent prompting is a training-free method and thus does not inherently degrade general capabilities.  
2. We provide an optimized training data format that balances the performance on both EgoGazeVQA and EgoSchema.
3. The benchmark is intentionally scoped for gaze-aware MLLMs, with non-gaze baselines included solely to calibrate the necessity of incorporating gaze.

comment.value:
Dear Area Chairs and Reviewer j14H,

Thank you again for your follow-up comments and suggestion. We understand your concern regarding dataset size, and would like to provide further context by comparing EgoGazeVQA to recent peer-reviewed video understanding benchmarks:

| Benchmark | Type |  Videos   | QA pairs |Citations | Year | Venue |
|-----------|:--------:| :--------:|:---------------:|:--------:|:--------:|:--------:| 
| Video-MME [1] | Exo |   900    |   2,700  |  478     |  2025           | CVPR
| MMWorld [2]   | Exo |   1,910    |   1,599    |   28      |   2025     | ICLR|
| Vidcomposition [3] | Exo |   982   |    1,706  |    9  |     2025       | CVPR|
| Q-Bench-Video [4]| Exo |  1,800| 2,378 |  9    |  2025 | CVPR|
| Lvbench [5] | Exo |   500   |    1,549   |    92  |     2024       | ICCV|
| Mmbench-video [6] | Exo   | 600  | 1,998  | 93 | 2024 | NeurIPS |
| VideoMindPalace [7]   | Ego   | 200  | 1,800  | 1 | 2025 | CVPR |
| EgoThink [8]      | Ego |  700  |  700 | 34 | 2024  | CVPR |
| **EgoGazeVQA(Ours)** | Ego | 913 | 1,757 | / | 2025| / |

As the table shows, our dataset EgoGazeVQA is within the same scale as recent peer-reviewed benchmarks. Moreover, Unlike most existing benchmarks, each QA pair in EgoGazeVQA is associated with  **gaze eye-tracking data**, which provides a valuable cue for MLLMs to better infer the user’s intent in egocentric settings.

We hope these clarifications address your concern. Thank you again for your valuable comments and thoughtful engagement!

Best,

The Authors

**Reference**

[1] Fu, Chaoyou, et al. "Video-mme: The first-ever comprehensive evaluation benchmark of multi-modal llms in video analysis." Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025.

[2] He, Xuehai, et al. "MMWorld: Towards Multi-discipline Multi-faceted World Model Evaluation in Videos." The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations.

[3] Tang, Yunlong, et al. "Vidcomposition: Can mllms analyze compositions in compiled videos?." Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025.

[4] Zhang, Zicheng, et al. "Q-Bench-Video: Benchmark the Video Quality Understanding of LMMs." Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025.

[5] Wang, Weihan, et al. "Lvbench: An extreme long video understanding benchmark." arXiv preprint arXiv:2406.08035 (2024).

[6] Fang, Xinyu, et al. "Mmbench-video: A long-form multi-shot benchmark for holistic video understanding." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (2024): 89098-89124.

[7] Huang, Zeyi, et al. "Building a Mind Palace: Structuring Environment-Grounded Semantic Graphs for Effective Long Video Analysis with LLMs." Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025.

[8] Cheng, Sijie, et al. "Egothink: Evaluating first-person perspective thinking capability of vision-language models." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2024.

We sincerely thank Reviewer j14H for constructive feedback, which have helped us improve our work. In response, we offer additional experimental results and explanations to address the suggestions raised by Reviewer j14H.

**Q1: The proposed EgoGazeVQA benchmark is limited in data size.**

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment on the benchmark size. We would like to point out that EgoTextVQA and EgoSchema do not require gaze tracking data. Since only a small portion of existing egocentric videos datasets contain high-quality gaze tracking data, it is challenging to scale up the benchmark size without introducing duplication. Despite such constraints, our EgoGazeVQA considers a richer collection of videos (913) compared to EgoThink (700) and EgoMemoria (629). Moreover, our dataset size (1757 QA pairs) is comparable to widely recognized video understanding benchmarks like LVBench[1] (1549 QA pairs) and MMBench-Video[2] (1998 QA pairs). 

**Q2: There is no simple baseline to address the challenges in EgoGazeVQA.**

We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion to include additional baselines. In Table 3 of the main paper, we report performance of representative MLLMs on EgoGazeVQA to establish demonstrative baselines and highlight the significant room for improvement on gaze-relevant tasks. Here, we provide results using CLIP (ViT-H-14) and EgoVLP as simple baselines, where we compute the cosine similarity between the visual embeddings of the input and the text embeddings of each answer option, selecting the one with the highest similarity as the prediction. We also evaluate BLIP-2, where generates answers based on the visual embeddings and input question. We calculate the cross-entropy loss between the generated answer and each of the candidate options, and select the one with the lowest loss as the most likely match.

For both baselines, we follow the same video preprocessing pipeline described in the main paper. To mimic human visual attention, we use gaze fixation as an attentional map to select around 20\% of each frame, resulting in what we term the GazeMap variant (i.e., CLIP-GazeMap, EgoVLP-GazeMap and BLIP-2-GazeMap), with all other components unchanged. 

| Method         |Similarity |  Performance | 
|----------------|:------:|:-------:|
| Human  |N/A |  76.8  |
| CLIP ViT-H-14  |Video-A |  21.63  |
|   CLIP-GazeMap |Video-A |  21.79  |
|     EgoVLP     |Video-A |  22.95  |
| EgoVLP-GazeMap |Video-A |  22.65  |
|     BLIP-2     |  N/A   |  27.60  |

|Qwen2.5-VL-72B  |  N/A   |  60.5   |
|Qwen2.5-VL-72B-GazeVisual | N/A| 63.9  |


Notably, these simple baselines perform only marginally better than random guessing and fall far short of human expert performance, indicating that CLIP-based methods struggle to tackle this challenging benchmark. Moreover, simply narrowing the visual field through gaze cropping proves insufficient for fully leveraging gaze information with existing vision encoders. This reinforces the need for the specialized prompting strategies proposed in our work, which incorporate spatiotemporal and intent-aware cues. We will incorporate this dicsusion in our main paper.

We thank the reviewer p3sj for recognizing the novelty, practical value and concerns. Below we address the two remaining concerns.
 
**Q1: Indoor bias and short‑video focus.**

We thank the reviewer for raising concerns regarding the generalizability of our benchmark. We provide further clarification:
 
* Limited outdoor gaze data due to hardware constraints. Current head‑mounted eye‑trackers (e.g., HoloAssist, Aria, Tobii Pro) depend on near‑infrared (NIR) illumination and the pupil–corneal reflection. In outdoor scenes, sun light and glasses can seriously disturb the reflective properties of IR light. Methods using IR can therefore be less reliable in these situations[1], while pupil constriction further reduces the signal. As a result, gaze tracking in outdoor scenes suffers from significant inaccuracies. These limitations are the reason existing egocentric datasets (e.g., Ego4D, EgoExo, EGTEA, HoloAssist-Aria) do not include outdoor gaze annotations.

* Short and medium-length videos (30s–2min) has been widely used in many egocentric activity understanding dataset (AssistQ[2], EgoSchema[3], EgoTextVQA[4]) and video language model benchmark (ActivityNet-QA[5], MMBench-Video[6]). Although long video understanding with gaze context is a promising direction, limitations the scarcity of egocentric video data with accurate eye-tracking signals, and high computational cost present additional challenges for academic research. We plan to further explore this direction in future work.

We will properly discuss these constraints upon the release of our benchmark.

**Q2: Inconsistencies on performance improvement and impact of gaze‑estimation error.**

Thank you for your suggestion. We acknowledge that the performance gains from gaze-guided prompting exhibit some inconsistencies. This actually highlights the challenging nature of our benchmark, which cannot be easily solved with gaze-guided prompting alone, and underscores the need for further attention and investigation from the community.

We also conducted a more detailed analysis at both the dataset level and category level. GT refers to using gaze ground truth in our prompting strategy, while GE refers to using gaze estimation.

| Datasets |  w/o(baseline) | GT | $\Delta$ (GT-w/o) |  GE | $\Delta$(GE-w/o) | MSE   |
|---------|:----:|:--:|:-----------------:|:---:|:----------------:|:-----:|
| Ego4D   | 60.1 | 67.0  | +6.9          | 60.5  | +0.4          | 0.154 |
| EgoExo  | 61.7 | 67.3  | +5.6          | 64.5  | +2.8          | 0.038 |
| EGTEA   | 59.3 | 64.0  | +4.7          | 58.7  | -0.6          | 0.119 |
| Avg.    | 60.5 | 66.3  | +5.8          | 61.5  | +1.0          | 0.099 |

In datasets level table, we see that in EGTEA, where gaze estimation is less accurate (MSE = 0.119), gaze-guided prompting does not improve performance and can even slightly hurt it. In contrast, when gaze prediction is accurate in EgoExo (MSE = 0.038), it brings a clear performance boost.

| Category | w/o(baseline)  | GT   | $\Delta$(GT - w/o) | GE   | $\Delta$(GE - w/o) |
| -------- | :----: | :----: | :------------: | :----: | :------------: |
| Spatial  | 57.1 | 64.3 | +7.2         | 53.8 | -3.3         |
| Temporal | 45.2 | 50.3 | +5.1         | 48.6 | +3.4         |
| Causal   | 79.4 | 84.3 | +4.9         | 82.2 | +2.8         |

From the results and visualizations, we can draw the following conclusions:

* We observe that gaze-guided prompting using gaze estimation leads to performance degradation in spatial questions. This suggests that spatial reasoning is highly sensitive to gaze estimation accuracy, as it often depends on precise spatial grounding. For instance, if the estimated gaze falls slightly off the object being manipulated—especially when nearby objects are close together, such as mistaking a knife for a cutting board—the model may misinterpret the target of the action and produce an incorrect response. 
* In contrast, temporal questions rely more on in-context temporal cues and are less affected by gaze estimation noise. Still, if the estimated gaze lands on a static background object rather than a newly appearing item, the model may miss key temporal transitions. 
* For causal reasoning, if the gaze is misestimated to a nearby object rather than the causal trigger (e.g., glancing at a mug instead of the hand turning on a kettle), the model might fail to infer the correct cause-effect relationship.

We will add these insights to our analysis section to further clarify the differential impact of gaze quality across reasoning types. We hope our response sufficiently addresses your comments. If you have any further questions or concerns, please feel free to reach out to us for further discussion.

A dataset for understanding complex web videos via question answering. In Proceedings of the AAAI

Similarly, in our context, there are several existing gaze-independent egocentric benchmarks that can be used to assess model generalization.

Specifically, we conducted an additional experiment to evaluate the effect of LoRA fine-tuning on gaze-independent QA. We evaluated a LoRA-tuned Qwen2.5-VL-7B model on EgoSchema, which does not contain gaze annotations and thus does not support our gaze-guided prompting strategy. summary.value: This paper innovatively introduces gaze points into the first-person perspective VQA process, designing both a training and a test dataset. It also explores three gaze-guided prompting strategies and validates them across various scenes and tasks, yielding some very interesting results.

strengths_contributions.value: This is the first paper to incorporate gaze into first-person VQA, making it a highly novel task that could potentially serve as an entry point for future human-computer interactions. The paper provides thorough validation across various models, including attempts to predict the gaze point, which led to notable performance improvements.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. In Table 7, the baseline is not marked, and results without gaze estimation are missing, which would be helpful for comparison.

2. There is no analysis of out-of-distribution (OOD) performance. For example, how would the model perform on general tasks after training on gaze-related QA? All the QA tasks in this paper are gaze-related, but in real-world usage of multimodal large models, this is not the problem distribution. I strongly recommend including gaze-independent questions in the test set.

3. I think the red and green arrows in Tables 4, 5, etc., are not very meaningful. All your QA questions are about things like "where did you look?" Without gaze information, the model can only guess randomly. When the number of targets is large, the probability of a correct guess is lower, and when the number of targets is small, the probability of a correct guess is higher. Therefore, the distribution of these tasks and scenes might just reflect the distribution of the number of targets, which may not have significant analytical value.

final_justification.value: I think the additional experiments and explanations have alleviated some of my concerns. Since this paper only proposes a training-free method for injecting gaze information through prompting, the supplementary experiments on “Textual Gaze Prompt + Question” also somehow demonstrate that this prompt is meaningful. I am inclined to give an accept score.

summary.value: This paper introduces EgoGazeVQA, a novel benchmark for egocentric gaze-guided video question answering. It aims to evaluate whether MLLMs can leverage gaze information to better interpret user intention from first-person videos. The benchmark is constructed from three popular egocentric video datasets, augmented with gaze data and automatically generated QA pairs verified by human annotators. The authors further explore three gaze-guided prompting strategies and evaluate several open- and closed-source MLLMs.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. Overall this paper is well-written and is easy to understand.
2 This paper introduce EgoGazeVQA, an egocentric gaze-guided VQA benchmark that leverages gaze information to improve the understanding of longer daily-life videos.
3. Experimental results demonstrate that  the effectiveness of gaze-guided intent prompting methods in EgoGazeVQA.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. There is no mention of how human performance compares to MLLMs on this benchmark. This makes it hard to judge whether the task is inherently ambiguous or model-limited.
2. Besides LoRA fine-tuning, could the authors also provide a comparison with full fine-tuning results?
3. We encourage the authors to provide a more detailed analysis of how gaze estimation errors impact model performance in specific spatial and temporal QA scenarios, which would offer deeper insights into the sensitivity of different reasoning tasks to gaze accuracy.

summary.value: This paper introduces "EgoGazeVQA," a novel benchmark for evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in understanding user intent from egocentric videos by incorporating gaze signals. Egocentric videos capture first-person perspectives, aligning visual perception, attention, and context, but existing benchmarks overlook gaze as a key indicator of intent. It addresses this gap by leveraging gaze data to generate spatial, temporal, and causal intent question-answering (QA) tasks.

strengths_contributions.value:
​1. Novelty and Significance: EgoGazeVQA is the first benchmark to integrate gaze signals for egocentric video intent understanding, filling a critical gap in MLLM evaluation. By focusing on spatial, temporal, and causal intent QA, it enables more personalized AI assistants, which is timely given the rise of wearable devices.

2. Rigorous Methodology: The benchmark construction is robust, using diverse datasets and human verification for QA pair quality. The experiments are comprehensive, covering multiple MLLMs and scenarios, with detailed metrics like accuracy and MSE. 

3. Practical Impact and Openness: The work has high practical value for developing intent-aware AI systems, with real-world applications in healthcare, gaming, and daily assistance. The authors provide full access to code and data, including detailed prompts and evaluation scripts, facilitating reproducibility and community adoption.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Data and Generalizability Limitations: The benchmark relies heavily on indoor scenarios, introducing bias and limiting generalizability to outdoor or dynamic environments. The focus on short to medium-length videos overlooks challenges in long-video processing, such as maintaining temporal coherence, which may reduce the benchmark's applicability to real-world streaming data.

​2. Implementation Gaps: The gaze-guided prompting strategies show performance gains but have inconsistencies; for example, salience maps excel in spatial intent but underperform in temporal tasks due to MLLMs' poor temporal correlation handling. The paper does not thoroughly address how gaze estimation inaccuracies impact prompting effectiveness, leaving a gap in error analysis.

summary.value: To address the issue of previous benchmarks neglecting the role of gaze in egocentric video understanding, this paper presents a new benchmark named EgoGazeVQA, which consists of egocentric gaze-guided video question answering. In addition, the authors also propose a gaze-guided intent prompting method to leverage spatial, temporal, and intent-related cues.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This paper first exploits egocentric gaze-guided video intent QA in the egocentric video understanding community.

2. This paper investigates gaze-guided prompting paradigms that leverage cues from spatial, temporal, and intent levels.

3. The authors present empirical analysis to validate the effectiveness of gaze signals in understanding human intentions in the egocentric field.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The proposed EgoGazeVQA benchmark is limited in data size. For example, EgoGazeVQA only has 1757 questions (1.7k), which is less than EgoSchema (5k) and EgoTextVQA (7k). This relatively small scale may hinder the robustness of the evaluation and limit the generalizability of models. The authors should include more diverse and comprehensive question-answer pairs.

2. This paper only provides some prompting strategies for this task, and there is no simple baseline to address the challenges in EgoGazeVQA. 

3. In the QA pair generation step, is there a risk of hallucination or factual inaccuracies propagating into the QA pairs? Have the authors evaluated the proportion of such errors?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
For suggestions, I think the authors should improve the dataset size of EgoGazeVQA to better capture the diversity and complexity of real-world egocentric gaze behaviors.

I have no additional questions.

final_justification.value:
The authors' response has addressed the majority of my concerns. 
Therefore, I raise my score to "Borderline accept".

title.value: In the Eye of MLLM: Benchmarking Egocentric Video Intent Understanding with Gaze-Guided Prompting

abstract.value: The emergence of advanced multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has significantly enhanced AI assistants' ability to process complex information across modalities. Recently, egocentric videos, by directly capturing user focus, actions, and context in an unified coordinate, offer an exciting opportunity to enable proactive and personalized AI user experiences with MLLMs. However, existing benchmarks overlook the crucial role of gaze as an indicator of user intent. To address this gap, we introduce EgoGazeVQA, an egocentric gaze-guided video question answering benchmark that leverages gaze information to improve the understanding of longer daily-life videos. EgoGazeVQA consists of gaze-based QA pairs generated by MLLMs and refined by human annotators. Our experiments reveal that existing MLLMs struggle to accurately interpret user intentions using only global visual tokens. In contrast, our gaze-guided intent prompting methods significantly enhance performance by integrating spatial, temporal, and intent-related cues. We further conduct experiments on gaze-related fine-tuning and analyze how gaze estimation accuracy impacts prompting effectiveness. These results underscore the value of gaze for more personalized and effective AI assistants in egocentric settings.
